rationale: A wins because it keeps four clean story shapes without pretending the update proves more than it does. Its strongest line, "How Brex built card issuing and local-currency reimbursement in 50 countries," gives a real infrastructure beat a real reporting path. B has good instincts, but "A $12.3B private fintech is spending on 50-country expansion without disclosing whether it makes money" leans too hard on cost, burn, and IPO tension the update does not substantiate. That is the difference between sharp pressure and invented edge.
gaps_in_A: "Brex expands corporate cards to 50 countries, opening a new front against Ramp and the banks" is usable, but it needs external competitor proof before anyone says "new front" with a straight face.

"Enterprise customers pushed Brex, the startup card company, to go global" depends heavily on Brex's own "top enterprise customer request" claim; A flags this, but the angle still lives or dies on a number it does not have.
The customer angle is properly shaped, but "The finance team that stopped wiring reimbursements across borders" risks implying wires were the actual before-state before a named customer confirms it.
A misses one legitimate pressure angle around private-company economics, though it correctly refuses the sloppier valuation-pressure version.
gaps_in_B: "multinational-payroll problem" is the wrong category. The update is cards, expenses, and reimbursement, not payroll.
"Brex bets 50 countries is the thing Ramp can't copy quickly" invents difficulty and strategic intent. The update says Brex competes with Ramp; it does not say Ramp cannot copy it quickly.
"after years of fighting over the same US venture-backed customer base" is outside the supplied facts and should not be smuggled in as context in a blind angle set.

"Multi-country issuing is not a cheap feature -- it implies licensing, partner banks, and local compliance headcount" may be plausible, but it turns inference into load-bearing proof for a funding-mechanics angle.
